claims.claim: Rob Fitzpatrick's The Mom Test (2013): talk about their life instead of your idea, ask about specifics in the past instead of opinions about the future, talk less and listen more; compliments, fluff and ideas are the three kinds of misleading data.
claims.source: Secondary summaries (Shortform, Unusual Ventures, Koji) found by search on 13 November 2026; the book itself was not checked.

claims.claim: Starting a requirements interview from the decision, and the A or B test, are common analytics practice.
claims.source: General practice, not a quotation from one source.

concept_html:
Requests arrive as solutions: "Build me an attrition dashboard." If you build what was asked, you often build the wrong thing. Before you start, run a short requirements interview.

Find the decision. Ask what decision the work will inform, who makes it and when. Then ask: "If the answer were A, what would you do? And if it were B?" If both answers lead to the same action, the analysis changes nothing. Say so, and save the effort.

Ask about the past, not the future. Rob Fitzpatrick's The Mom Test (2013) gives three rules for interviews that people answer politely but unhelpfully:

  • Talk about their work, not your idea.
  • Ask about specific events in the past, not opinions about the future. "The last time you reviewed attrition, what did you look at, and what did you do next?" beats "Would you use a dashboard?"
  • Talk less and listen more.

Filter bad data. Three kinds of answer mislead you. Compliments ("that sounds great") tell you nothing. Fluff is generic or hypothetical ("we always", "we would"): ask for the last real example. Feature requests ("add a filter by grade") hide a motive: ask what the filter would let them do.

Close with a written brief. Record the decision, the decision-maker, the date it is needed, how often, the data sources and their owners, and how you will know the work succeeded. Send it back and ask for corrections. A brief the requester has confirmed protects you both when scope grows.

lines: Q: The last time you reviewed attrition, what did you look at?
A: The quarterly board pack. I picked three teams for a retention review.
Q: How did you pick them?
A: Highest leaver counts. Small teams always looked fine.
Q: If a small team lost half its people, would you review it?
A: Yes. I never saw them.
Brief: decision = which teams get a retention review, owner = HR director,
needed = each quarter, two weeks before the board, data = HR system
(owner: HRIS lead), success = no team over 20% loss is missed.

notes.html: A specific past event, not an opinion about the future.
The real problem: counts hide small teams. Rates would show them.
The brief starts from the decision, with an owner, a date and a success measure.

example.takeaway_html: Ask what decision a request serves, who makes it and when. Interview about specific past events, filter out compliments, fluff and feature requests, and confirm a written brief.

lines: Q: Would you use an attrition dashboard?
A: Yes, that would be great.
Q: What filters do you want?
A: Grade, site, tenure, manager, gender, everything really.
Brief: attrition dashboard with all filters.

A compliment. It tells you nothing about what they will do.
No decision, no owner, no date and no measure of success.

title: Find the decision behind the request
why_html: A team spent six weeks building an attrition dashboard with 14 filters. The HR director opened it twice. The real need was a quarterly answer to one question: which teams need a retention review. A one-page list, refreshed each quarter, would have taken three days.
